Appendix Contents

Appendix A Additional Architecture Details

A.1 OptScientist Model

The OptScientist Model implements the two-stage discovery procedure introduced in Sec. 3.2. The Optimization Learner (OptLearner) first learns to represent observational data as an optimization problem, and the Optimization Discoverer (OptDiscover) subsequently extracts its symbolic form. The discrete- and continuous-outcome implementations share the same model architecture, optimization procedure, validation protocol, and symbolic-distillation pipeline. They differ primarily in how candidate decisions are constructed for the OptLearner training objective.

OptLearner architecture.

OptLearner uses the Behavior Learning Network (BL) as its backbone to learn a scalar optimization landscape over context–outcome pairs. For each context xx and candidate outcome yy, the network returns a score Sθ​(x,y)S_{\theta}(x,y) that measures how strongly yy is preferred under the latent optimization problem.

Building on the BL backbone, OptLearner represents observational data as a single optimization problem. Its early layers denoise and compress observations, capturing interactions and latent features that may be difficult to express in the original coordinates. The final layer consists of a single BL block, forming an optimization representation bottleneck with learnable objective and optional constraint components, each potentially comprising multiple branches,

maxy∈𝒴⁡Uθ​(x,y)⏟[λ0]s.t.Cθ​(x,y)⏟[λ1]≤0,Tθ​(x,y)⏟[λ2]=0.\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\underbrace{U_{\theta}(x,y)}_{[\lambda_{0}]}\quad\mathrm{s.t.}\quad\underbrace{C_{\theta}(x,y)}_{[\lambda_{1}]}\leq 0,\qquad\underbrace{T_{\theta}(x,y)}_{[\lambda_{2}]}=0. (10)

Here λ0\lambda_{0} controls the scale of the objective, while λ1\lambda_{1} and λ2\lambda_{2} control the strengths of the inequality and equality terms. This bottleneck provides a structured optimization representation for subsequent symbolic discovery. When the input variables are already meaningful, OptLearner primarily denoises the optimization landscape. For high-dimensional or weakly structured inputs, it additionally extracts and compresses relevant features before forming the learned optimization representation.

In the default implementation, OptLearner contains two BL layers with widths [128,1][128,1]. The first layer uses one UU branch and one CC branch, and the default final block contains a single UU branch. This configuration provides the default single-objective form used in the main OptFeynman experiments. Task-specific configurations can additionally activate CC and TT in the final block, as in the constrained OptScientist variants used in our experiments.

Unified learning objective.

The discrete and continuous implementations can be written using the same candidate-ranking objective. For observation (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}), let 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} denote the set of candidate decisions considered during that training step. OptLearner minimizes

ℒOptLearner=−1N∑i=1Nlogexp⁡(Sθ​(xi,yi)/τ)∑y∈𝒜iexp⁡(Sθ​(xi,y)/τ).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OptLearner}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\exp\!\left(S_{\theta}(x_{i},y_{i})/\tau\right)}{\sum_{y\in\mathcal{A}_{i}}\exp\!\left(S_{\theta}(x_{i},y)/\tau\right)}. (11)

For discrete outcomes, 𝒜i=𝒴\mathcal{A}_{i}=\mathcal{Y} and the model evaluates the complete finite decision set, giving the cross-entropy objective in Eq. (11). For continuous outcomes, OptLearner constructs a sampled candidate set,

𝒜i={yi,y~i​1,…,y~i​K},y~i​k∼Unif⁡(𝒴),\mathcal{A}_{i}=\left\{y_{i},\widetilde{y}_{i1},\ldots,\widetilde{y}_{iK}\right\},\qquad\widetilde{y}_{ik}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{Y}), (12)

where the observed outcome is compared with KK alternatives sampled uniformly from the feasible decision range. This gives the sampled contrastive Gibbs objective in Eq. (6). Both settings therefore train the same latent optimization score by assigning higher scores to observed outcomes than to feasible alternatives under the same context.

OptLearner is optimized on the training split and selected using validation loss. The best checkpoint is updated whenever validation loss improves. Training terminates after the specified number of consecutive epochs without validation improvement or when the maximum number of epochs is reached. The checkpoint with the lowest validation loss is then restored and frozen before symbolic discovery.

OptDiscover implementation.

After OptLearner is trained, its parameters are frozen. OptDiscover extracts the symbolic form of the learned optimization problem by distilling the components of the optimization representation bottleneck. For each active component

Hθ,j∈{Uθ,Cθ,Tθ},H_{\theta,j}\in\{U_{\theta},C_{\theta},T_{\theta}\},

the model generates a distillation dataset over context–decision pairs and records the corresponding learned component values. Symbolic regression then searches for an expression

H^j=arg⁡minF∈ℱΩj​1M​∑m=1M[F⁡(xm,ym)−Hθ,j​(xm,ym)]2,\widehat{H}_{j}=\arg\min_{F\in\mathcal{F}_{\Omega_{j}}}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left[F(x_{m},y_{m})-H_{\theta,j}(x_{m},y_{m})\right]^{2}, (13)

where ℱΩj\mathcal{F}_{\Omega_{j}} denotes the symbolic search space for the jj-th component.

The symbolic language Ωj\Omega_{j} is task-dependent. We use a compact base operator set by default, and additional binary or unary operators can be introduced when required by the scientific problem or by explicit search priors. This design allows the symbolic hypothesis space to reflect the mathematical structure of each discovery task.

Symbolic search is performed separately for the active components of the optimization representation bottleneck. The resulting expressions are assembled according to the learned optimization structure, yielding a compact symbolic optimization problem with an explicit objective and optional constraints. Among expressions with near-minimal distillation loss, OptDiscover selects the expression with the lowest effective symbolic complexity. For the objective component, additive terms that depend only on xx are subsequently removed because they remain constant across candidate decisions and therefore do not affect the optimizer. The retained symbolic components define the final discovered optimization law.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the common implementation for discrete and continuous outcomes.

Implementation and hyperparameters.

Table 2 reports the default implementation settings used in our experiments. These values specify the base OptLearner and OptDiscover configuration. The active U/C/TU/C/T structure and symbolic operator language can vary across task-specific configurations. The operator entries in the table report the default symbolic search language.

The symbolic-search settings provide a base configuration that can be adapted to the scientific structure of each task. In particular, Ω\Omega can be expanded with task-relevant operators before OptDiscover is executed. This allows the OptLearner architecture to remain common across tasks while the symbolic hypothesis space adapts to each scientific domain.

A.2 OptScientist Agent

The OptScientist Agent implements the iterative scientific-discovery process introduced in Sec. 3.3. A Research Orchestrator maintains the research state and coordinates three specialized agents: a Theory Prior Agent, an Experiment Agent, and a Scientific Critic and Theory Abstraction Agent. Together, these components connect scientific reasoning with model training, symbolic discovery and empirical evaluation, allowing candidate optimization laws to be progressively proposed, tested, adjudicated and abstracted.

The architecture is organized around a shared research state that accumulates information across discovery rounds. This state contains the research question, variable definitions, theoretical hypotheses, fixed data split, search configurations, discovered symbolic laws, evaluation results and unresolved scientific questions. Maintaining these elements in a common state allows later stages to trace each candidate law back to the assumptions, variables and empirical evidence that produced it. It also enables the system to preserve informative failures: unstable symbolic structures, weakly supported mechanisms and missing explanatory variables can directly shape the next round of discovery.

Each specialized agent operates on a role-specific view of this state and returns structured outputs to the Research Orchestrator. Scientific priors therefore enter the workflow as explicit hypotheses and search constraints; empirical results enter through executed OptScientist runs; and scientific interpretations are formed from the accumulated evidence across candidate laws.

Embedding the OptScientist Model in the discovery loop. The OptScientist Model forms the empirical core of the agentic discovery system. In each discovery round, the Theory Prior Agent converts scientific knowledge into a structured set of candidate hypotheses, variables and search priors. These outputs can include newly constructed variables, transformations of observed variables, candidate mechanisms, preferred symbolic operators and restrictions on admissible functional forms. The Experiment Agent combines these proposals with model and training parameters to construct a bounded set of executable OptScientist runs.

Concretely, each run is represented by a configuration

Qk=(𝒱k,ℳk,Θk,Ωk),Q_{k}=\left(\mathcal{V}_{k},\,\mathcal{M}_{k},\,\Theta_{k},\,\Omega_{k}\right),

where 𝒱k\mathcal{V}_{k} denotes the observed and theory-derived variables supplied to the model, ℳk\mathcal{M}_{k} specifies the OptScientist representation to be fitted, Θk\Theta_{k} contains the corresponding model, training and search parameters, and Ωk\Omega_{k} defines the symbolic language used for distillation. For example, a prior analysis of the data informed by the scientific literature may suggest an expected-reward variable or a particular interaction between observed quantities. The Experiment Agent adds these variables to the corresponding model input, assigns an OptLearner architecture and training configuration, specifies the operators available to OptDiscover, and submits the resulting configuration as an OptScientist run. Different hypotheses, variable sets or parameter settings can therefore generate complementary runs within the same discovery round.

Figure 9 summarizes this interface. Scientific proposals are first converted into executable configurations. These configurations are passed to the OptScientist Model, which learns an optimization representation and distills it into symbolic laws. The resulting laws and their empirical evidence are then returned to the research state for scientific adjudication and refinement.

Each configuration is evaluated using the two-stage OptScientist Model introduced in Sec. 3.2. Given the training data restricted to the variables in 𝒱k\mathcal{V}_{k}, OptLearner fits a scalar optimization landscape,

Sθk=OptLearner​(𝒟train​[𝒱k],ℳk,Θk).S_{\theta_{k}}=\textsc{OptLearner}\left(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}[\mathcal{V}_{k}],\mathcal{M}_{k},\Theta_{k}\right).

The learned hierarchy can denoise observations, compress redundant information, or construct intermediate representations, which are then expressed as a single optimization problem through the optimization representation bottleneck. The fitted model therefore provides a data-driven representation of how candidate outcomes are ranked under the observed contexts.

After training, the OptLearner parameters are frozen. OptDiscover receives the learned optimization representation together with the symbolic specification Ωk\Omega_{k} and distills its components into compact symbolic expressions,

ℒk=OptDiscover​(Sθk,Ωk).\mathcal{L}_{k}=\textsc{OptDiscover}\left(S_{\theta_{k}},\Omega_{k}\right).

For a single-objective configuration, this procedure distills the learned objective directly. For a constrained configuration, the objective, inequality-constraint and equality-constraint components are distilled separately and then assembled according to the learned optimization structure. The symbolic-search specification controls the admissible operators and functional forms, while the distillation loss and complexity criterion determine which candidate expressions are retained.

The Experiment Agent collects the output of every successful run as an evidence package,

ℰk=(CLOSE\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{k}=\bigl( validation performance,symbolic complexity,\displaystyle\text{validation performance},\text{symbolic complexity},
OPENdistillation fidelity,run stability,execution record).\displaystyle\text{distillation fidelity},\text{run stability},\text{execution record}\bigr).

The pair (ℒk,ℰk)(\mathcal{L}_{k},\mathcal{E}_{k}) is written back to the shared research state. Repeated symbolic searches can contribute several low-complexity expressions with near-optimal distillation loss, allowing alternative structures to remain available when the data do not identify a unique symbolic form. The resulting candidate set therefore records both the discovered mathematical expressions and the evidence supporting each expression.

The Scientific Critic and Theory Abstraction Agent receives these candidate laws together with their evidence records and the hypotheses that generated the corresponding runs. It compares candidates using predictive performance, symbolic complexity, fidelity to the learned optimization landscape and stability across repeated searches, and identifies the laws and mathematical structures that receive the strongest empirical support. It then abstracts these supported structures into a more general theoretical form and summarizes the corresponding qualitative mechanisms and scientific findings. The exact candidate expressions are retained alongside this abstraction, preserving the connection between the empirical laws and the higher-level theory derived from them.

Remaining uncertainty is translated into concrete modifications of the next discovery round. These may include introducing a new theoretically motivated variable, removing a redundant representation, changing the symbolic operator set, evaluating an alternative OptScientist configuration or requesting additional observations. The resulting theory abstraction, mechanism findings and refinement proposals are written back to the shared research state and used to define the subsequent round of discovery.

This interface creates a direct path from scientific reasoning to model execution and back to scientific interpretation. Theory-guided variables, hypotheses and search priors are compiled by the Experiment Agent into explicit OptScientist configurations; OptLearner and OptDiscover recover candidate optimization laws from the data; and the resulting evidence is evaluated by the Scientific Critic and Theory Abstraction Agent. The supported laws are then adjudicated, abstracted into a more general theoretical form and summarized as qualitative mechanisms and scientific findings. These conclusions, together with the remaining uncertainties, determine how the subsequent discovery round is refined.

Algorithm 2 makes this interface explicit.

Research Orchestrator. The Research Orchestrator provides the control layer of the discovery process. It maintains the shared research state, coordinates information transfer among agents, manages the search budget and determines whether another discovery round is needed. The state records theoretical hypotheses, accepted variables, model configurations, discovered symbolic expressions, their empirical evaluations, theory abstractions and qualitative findings, creating a persistent scientific record across successive rounds.

This persistent state also provides continuity between scientific reasoning and empirical search. A hypothesis proposed early in the workflow remains associated with the variables introduced to test it, the model configurations used during discovery and the evidence obtained from the resulting symbolic laws. Similarly, unresolved mechanisms identified by the Scientific Critic can be translated into explicit requests for additional variables, alternative transformations or further model searches. The Orchestrator therefore allows the discovery process to accumulate evidence over time while preserving the provenance of intermediate scientific decisions.

Importantly, the Orchestrator also preserves the boundary between scientific reasoning and model execution. Agent outputs that define hypotheses, variables or search priors are converted into explicit OptScientist configurations before model fitting. Conversely, outputs from OptLearner and OptDiscover enter subsequent agent reasoning only through recorded candidate laws and their associated empirical evidence. This separation makes it possible to distinguish structures proposed as theoretical priors from structures that are subsequently supported by model fitting and symbolic discovery.

Agent instructions. Each specialized agent is assigned a defined scientific role, information scope and output structure. The prompts emphasize testable hypotheses, executable empirical search and evidence-grounded scientific abstraction. Their principal instructions are summarized below.

Theory Prior Agent Role. Act as a scientific theorist preparing an optimization-law discovery problem. Input. Research question, decision variable, available variables, compact training-side data structure and allowed variable transformations. Instructions. Identify established scientific theories and mechanisms relevant to the research question and connect them to observed variables without treating theoretical priors as empirical conclusions. Formulate a small set of explicit and testable mechanism hypotheses. Identify scientifically meaningful, target-independent variables or derived variables that provide observable representations of these mechanisms, and propose sparse symbolic-search priors over operators and functional structures when scientifically justified. Exclude variable constructions that depend on the observed target or validation and test information, and examine identifiability, redundancy and other theoretical risks. Express each proposal in a form that can be evaluated through subsequent model fitting and symbolic discovery. Output. Background theory, mechanism hypotheses, candidate variables, theoretical rationale, symbolic-search priors, potential risks and unresolved scientific questions.

The Theory Prior Agent provides the scientific entry point to the discovery loop. Its role is particularly important when raw observations admit many possible representations. Domain concepts can suggest target-independent transformations that expose latent mechanisms, such as temporal differences, relative quantities, interaction terms or state variables. These proposals constrain the effective hypothesis space presented to symbolic discovery and provide an interpretable correspondence between discovered mathematical terms and candidate scientific mechanisms. Because the proposals remain explicit in the shared state, later stages can evaluate whether the resulting evidence supports, weakens or leaves each hypothesis unresolved.

The Theory Prior Agent does not determine the functional form of the final law. Its proposals define the scientific search space presented to OptScientist: which observed or derived variables may represent a mechanism, and which symbolic structures are scientifically plausible enough to prioritize during discovery. Whether those variables enter the final optimization law, and in what mathematical form, is determined subsequently by OptLearner and OptDiscover from the observational data.

Experiment Agent Role. Translate scientific priors into an empirical search for symbolic optimization laws. Input. Theory priors, validated variables, task type, available OptScientist configurations, symbolic operators, fixed validation protocol and compute budget. Instructions. Organize the theoretical mechanisms, proposed variables and symbolic-search priors into a bounded set of complementary OptScientist configurations. For each configuration, invoke OptLearner to fit the latent optimization landscape on the fixed training data and then invoke OptDiscover to distil the trained optimization representation into compact symbolic laws. Evaluate the resulting laws under the fixed validation protocol. Repeat symbolic discovery where useful for assessing structural stability, and preserve low-complexity, near-optimal complete expressions from each successful symbolic-search run rather than retaining only a single run-level expression. When variable construction fails, repair only the implementation while preserving its scientific meaning and target independence. Record the resulting candidate expressions, predictive performance, symbolic complexity, distillation evidence, repeated-run evidence and execution records. Preserve alternative high-performing structures for subsequent scientific adjudication rather than selecting the final scientific law. Output. OptScientist configurations, candidate symbolic optimization laws, predictive metrics, symbolic complexity, distillation and repeated-run evidence, execution records and runtime issues.

The Experiment Agent provides the empirical interface between scientific reasoning and the OptScientist Model. Candidate hypotheses are not evaluated by asking the language model to directly write a final equation. Instead, the agent converts each hypothesis into an executable discovery configuration specifying the candidate variables, model structure, symbolic operators and relevant search settings. This produces a small set of scientifically differentiated model runs that can be compared under the same training and validation protocol.

Each run then follows the fixed internal logic of the OptScientist Model. OptLearner receives the observational variables selected for that configuration and learns a scalar optimization landscape Sθ​(𝐱,𝐲)S_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}). Depending on the structure of the observations, OptLearner may primarily denoise meaningful scientific variables or additionally extract and compress features from high-dimensional or weakly structured inputs. Its final layer consists of a single BL block, forming an optimization representation bottleneck that represents the data as a single optimization problem. OptDiscover then extracts the symbolic form of the learned optimization problem.

After OptLearner has been trained, its parameters are frozen and OptDiscover operates on the learned representation rather than directly fitting the observed target. For a constrained representation, the learned objective, inequality-constraint and equality-constraint components are distilled separately and then assembled into a symbolic optimization problem. For a single-objective representation, the corresponding learned objective is distilled directly. The symbolic operators and structural priors proposed earlier in the discovery round determine the candidate symbolic language, while the distillation objective and complexity control determine which expressions are retained. This division of labour is important: the agent specifies the scientific search problem, whereas OptScientist learns and distills the optimization structure supported by the data.

The resulting evidence extends beyond predictive performance. Each symbolic-search run can contribute several low-complexity expressions with near-optimal distillation loss, allowing alternative structures to remain available when the symbolic evidence does not identify a unique expression. Candidate laws are therefore compared using their validation performance, symbolic complexity, fidelity to the learned optimization representation and stability across repeated searches. Recording these dimensions provides the Scientific Critic with evidence about both empirical adequacy and structural reliability, while preserving multiple competitive expressions when the available data do not clearly distinguish among them.

This explicit model interface also separates model discovery from scientific adjudication. The Experiment Agent records successful and unsuccessful runs but does not choose which expression should be interpreted as the final scientific law. Candidate-law adjudication, theory abstraction and mechanism-level interpretation occur only after the candidate expressions and their associated evidence have been returned to the shared research state.

Scientific Critic and Theory Abstraction Agent Role. Evaluate discovered optimization laws as candidate scientific explanations and abstract their best-supported scientific structure. Input. Theory hypotheses, candidate symbolic laws, validation evidence, symbolic complexity, distillation evidence, repeated-run stability and available robustness evidence. Instructions. Compare candidate laws using their empirical evidence and characterize the level of support for each proposed mechanism. Adjudicate among candidate laws by jointly considering predictive performance, symbolic complexity, structural stability and consistency with plausible theoretical mechanisms, while treating theory as a prior rather than a substitute for empirical support. Preserve the exact selected candidate expressions and identify structures and qualitative mechanisms that recur across supported laws. Synthesize the supported candidates into a general-to-specific theory abstraction, progressing from a general optimization form to supported functional structure, exact parameterized laws and qualitative findings. Assess explicit research hypotheses, identify competing explanations, limitations and remaining failure modes, and propose additional variables, observations or targeted analyses that could resolve the remaining scientific uncertainty. Output. Candidate-law adjudication, supported symbolic laws, general-to-specific theory abstraction, qualitative mechanisms, hypothesis assessment, limitations and targeted suggestions for subsequent discovery.

The Scientific Critic connects symbolic recovery to theory formation. Symbolic regression can produce several expressions with similar predictive performance, including algebraically related forms and model-specific residual terms. The Critic evaluates these expressions collectively and identifies structures that remain stable across supported candidates. Recurring structures provide evidence for mechanism-level conclusions, whereas unstable or weakly identified terms are retained as sources of uncertainty.

The Critic receives the output of OptScientist as empirical evidence rather than as a finished theory. This distinction allows it to compare not only the symbolic expressions themselves but also how faithfully they reproduce the learned optimization landscape, how well they generalize under the fixed validation protocol, and whether similar structures reappear across repeated discovery runs. Scientific interpretation is therefore conditioned on the evidence produced by the model rather than on the plausibility of an expression in isolation.

Theory abstraction is performed hierarchically. At the highest level, the Critic identifies the general optimization principle expressed by the supported laws, such as reward maximization, target tracking or minimization of a deviation cost. It then constructs a parameter-tied general form where common parameter structure is empirically supported, followed by the specific functional structure associated with interpretable mechanisms. The exact parameterized candidate laws are retained at the next level, preserving their empirical expressions, and the final level summarizes the supported qualitative findings. This hierarchy allows OptScientist to synthesize candidate laws into a more general form and qualitative mechanisms while preserving the detailed mathematical structure from which those conclusions were derived.

The Critic also converts unresolved evidence into new scientific questions. A missing mechanism may motivate a new derived variable; competing symbolic structures may motivate additional observations capable of distinguishing their predictions; and systematic prediction failures may indicate omitted context or an insufficient symbolic language. These outputs are returned to the shared research state and provide structured inputs for a subsequent discovery round. In the next round, the Theory Prior and Experiment Agents translate these unresolved questions into revised variables, hypotheses or OptScientist configurations, so that scientific critique produces a concrete change in the subsequent model search rather than remaining a purely textual assessment.

Overall, the architecture organizes OptScientist into an iterative sequence of theory formation, model-based empirical discovery, evidence evaluation and theory abstraction. The Theory Prior Agent establishes candidate mechanisms, scientifically meaningful representations and symbolic-search priors. The Experiment Agent converts these proposals into executable configurations and invokes the OptScientist Model. Within each run, OptLearner learns to represent observational data as an optimization problem through an optimization representation bottleneck, and OptDiscover then distills the learned representation into a compact symbolic optimization law. The Scientific Critic then adjudicates among the resulting candidates and synthesizes their supported structure into more general optimization forms and qualitative mechanisms. The Research Orchestrator preserves the connection between these stages and carries unresolved scientific questions across iterations. This division of labour places a specialized symbolic-discovery model at the empirical centre of the agentic workflow, allowing language-model agents to guide and interpret discovery without substituting linguistic generation for model-based evidence.

Appendix B Additional Experimental Details

B.1 Baselines

We compare OptScientist with standard machine-learning models, symbolic regression, optimization-structured models, domain-specific models, and three LLM-based automated model-discovery methods. The general baselines include Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) (Rumelhart et al., 1986), Logistic Regression (LR) (Cox, 1958), Random Forest (RF) (Breiman, 2001), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), Gradient-Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT) (Friedman, 2001), Symbolic Regression (SR) (Cranmer, 2023), Neural Energy-Based Models (Neural EBM) (LeCun et al., 2006), and Behavior Learning (BL) (Ma et al., 2026a). The LLM-based baselines are an LLM-only researcher, GeCCo (Rmus et al., 2026) as a code-assisted LLM approach, and Model Discovery Agent (Murphy, 2026, MDA;) as a Bayesian experiment-design approach.

OptFeynman. For OptFeynman, we compare against MLP, LR, RF, XGBoost, and GBDT as standard machine-learning baselines, SR as a direct symbolic-discovery baseline, Neural EBM and BL as optimization-structured baselines, and the three LLM-based baselines.

Human decisions under risk and ambiguity. For CPC18, we compare against established behavioural models, including expected-value logit, expected-utility logit, prospect-theory logit with fixed or fitted parameters, and mean–variance logit. We additionally include GBDT, MLP, RF, and XGBoost as machine-learning baselines, together with the three LLM-based baselines.

Central-bank monetary decisions. For monetary-policy decisions, we compare against MLP, RF, XGBoost, and GBDT as machine-learning baselines, Neural EBM as an optimization-structured baseline, SR as a direct symbolic-discovery baseline, and the three LLM-based baselines.

B.2 OptFeynman Ground-Truth Recovery

Statistical analysis. We report additional statistics for the OptFeynman experiments in Figures 3 and 4. The analysis uses results from the OptLearner score and the final OptScientist symbolic law produced by OptDiscover for 99 OptFeynman problems under each combination of decision type (discrete or continuous) and training condition. Throughout this section, OptLearner score refers to the learned optimization score before symbolic distillation, and OptScientist law refers to the final symbolic optimization law produced by OptDiscover. We use Clean for the original OptFeynman setting and Noisy-context for the noisy-context version defined in Sec. 5.1, in which Gaussian noise is added only to the training contexts. Each problem is treated as one observation when computing statistics across the benchmark. One duplicated record in the continuous Clean setting contained identical metrics and was counted once.

Recovery is evaluated using exact-order accuracy, pairwise preference accuracy, and the Gibbs distribution induced by the recovered score. Exact-order accuracy measures agreement between the complete preference order produced by the recovered and ground-truth objectives. Pairwise accuracy measures agreement across individual pairs of candidate outcomes. For continuous tasks, preference recovery is evaluated at K=10K=10, 5050, and 100100 candidate outcomes, and distribution recovery is evaluated on a dense grid over the decision interval.

Unless stated otherwise, reported uncertainty is the standard error across the 99 OptFeynman problems,

SE=sn,n=99,\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad n=99,

where ss is the sample standard deviation across problems. Error bars in Figures 3 and 4 use mean ±1\pm 1 SE. Medians and interquartile ranges are also reported for metrics with uneven distributions across problems. Perfect exact-order recovery denotes a task with exact-order accuracy equal to one.

Perfect exact-order recovery. Table 3 summarizes perfect ground-truth recovery. For discrete outcomes, OptScientist recovers the complete ground-truth preference order on 88/9988/99 Clean problems and 92/9992/99 Noisy-context problems. For continuous outcomes, it achieves perfect recovery on 78/9978/99 Clean problems and 76/9976/99 Noisy-context problems at K=10K=10, 5050, and 100100. The stability of these counts as KK increases shows that the recovered laws from OptScientist continue to preserve the full ordering over increasingly dense sets of candidate outcomes.

The learned OptLearner score has substantially fewer perfectly recovered problems. In the continuous Clean setting, the count decreases from 30/9930/99 at K=10K=10 to 14/9914/99 at K=100K=100. This difference is also visible in the discrete setting, where OptLearner achieves perfect recovery on 31/9931/99 Clean problems and 27/9927/99 Noisy-context problems.

Continuous outcomes. Table 4 reports continuous preference recovery. Under the Clean condition, mean OptScientist exact-order accuracy is 0.9000.900 at K=10K=10, 0.8710.871 at K=50K=50, and 0.8660.866 at K=100K=100. The corresponding values under Noisy-context are 0.9020.902, 0.8740.874, and 0.8690.869.

For every value of KK, the median and both quartiles of OptScientist exact-order accuracy are equal to one. Most problems therefore retain perfect ordering even when the candidate set becomes substantially denser. Pairwise recovery is similarly stable. Mean OptScientist pairwise accuracy remains approximately 0.960.96 across all candidate-set sizes and both training conditions, with a median of one.

OptLearner also achieves high pairwise accuracy, while its exact-order accuracy decreases more strongly with KK. Under the Clean condition, mean OptLearner exact-order accuracy decreases from 0.8250.825 at K=10K=10 to 0.7190.719 at K=100K=100.

The recovered continuous laws from OptScientist also preserve the Gibbs distributions generated by the ground-truth objectives. Mean dense-grid KL divergence is 0.04610.0461 under Clean and 0.04600.0460 under Noisy-context. The corresponding medians are 0.00800.0080 and 0.00710.0071, showing low distributional error for most tasks. OptLearner achieves mean KL values of 0.00780.0078 and 0.00820.0082, consistent with its direct fit to the stochastic optimization landscape.

Discrete outcomes. The discrete results show a similar pattern. Under the Clean condition, the recovered OptScientist laws achieve mean exact-order accuracy 0.9710.971 and pairwise accuracy 0.9840.984. Under Noisy-context, these values are 0.9740.974 and 0.9840.984. The median and both quartiles of OptScientist exact-order accuracy are equal to one in both conditions.

Training-context noise produces little change in the overall recovery statistics. Mean OptScientist exact-order accuracy changes from 0.9710.971 to 0.9740.974, while mean pairwise accuracy remains approximately 0.9840.984. The number of perfectly recovered tasks changes from 88/9988/99 to 92/9992/99. These results are consistent with the robustness observed in Figure 4.

For the Gibbs distributions over the five candidate actions, we additionally report probability MAE, defined as the mean absolute error between the ground-truth and recovered Gibbs probabilities across candidate actions. The OptScientist laws achieve mean probability MAE 0.01820.0182 and mean KL divergence 0.02170.0217 under the Clean condition. Their medians are 0.01150.0115 and 0.00360.0036, respectively. Under Noisy-context, mean probability MAE remains low at 0.02080.0208, with a median of 0.01170.0117. Mean OptScientist KL increases to 0.20050.2005, while the median remains 0.00360.0036 and the third quartile is 0.01320.0132. The difference between the mean and median reflects a small number of tasks with large KL values.

Effect of OptDiscover complexity control. Here we evaluate the expression-level reduction used within the symbolic complexity control of OptDiscover described in Sec. 3.2.2. In Table 9, Initial denotes the recovered symbolic expression before this reduction, and Final denotes the compact symbolic expression after it. We additionally compare exact-order recovery before and after this reduction. Discrete recovery is unchanged: mean exact-order accuracy remains 0.9710.971 under Clean and 0.9740.974 under Noisy-context, with 8888 and 9292 perfectly recovered problems, respectively.

For continuous outcomes, complexity control gives small improvements in exact-order recovery. Under Clean, mean accuracy increases by 0.0100.010, 0.0110.011, and 0.0130.013 at K=10K=10, 5050, and 100100. At K=100K=100, the number of perfectly recovered problems increases from 6767 to 7878. Under Noisy-context, changes in mean accuracy range from −0.001-0.001 to +0.005+0.005, and perfect recovery at K=100K=100 increases from 7070 to 7676 problems.

Held-out baseline comparison. Tables 10 and 11 report ground-truth recovery for the baseline models on unseen test contexts. The largest separation appears in exact-order recovery, which requires the recovered score to preserve the complete preference order induced by the ground-truth objective. In the discrete Clean setting, the two strongest baselines by mean exact-order accuracy are BL and logistic regression. BL achieves mean exact-order accuracy 0.8050.805 with perfect recovery on 31.3%31.3\% of tasks, and logistic regression achieves 0.7160.716 with perfect recovery on 17.2%17.2\%. OptScientist reaches 0.9710.971 exact-order accuracy and perfectly recovers 88/9988/99 tasks. The separation becomes larger for continuous outcomes as the candidate set grows. At K=100K=100, the two strongest baselines by mean exact-order accuracy, BL and Neural EBM, achieve exact-order accuracies of 0.7190.719 and 0.2940.294, with perfect recovery on 14.1%14.1\% and 10.1%10.1\% of tasks, respectively. OptScientist retains exact-order accuracy 0.8660.866 and perfectly recovers 78/9978/99 tasks.

Pairwise and distributional metrics provide complementary views of recovery. Several baselines preserve a substantial fraction of pairwise comparisons or closely approximate the Gibbs distribution while showing considerably weaker recovery of the complete ordering. For example, Neural EBM reaches pairwise accuracy 0.8880.888 and dense-grid KL divergence 0.00980.0098 at K=100K=100 in the continuous Clean setting, while its exact-order accuracy is 0.2940.294. BL achieves a dense-grid KL divergence of 0.00780.0078, lower than that achieved by OptScientist, while its exact-order accuracy decreases to 0.7190.719 at K=100K=100. A similar pattern appears for the LLM-only baseline in the discrete Clean setting, which reaches KL divergence 0.01250.0125 but exact-order accuracy 0.5880.588, with perfect recovery on only 5.1%5.1\% of tasks. These results show that accurate approximation of local pairwise relations or the stochastic landscape can coexist with substantial errors in the complete preference order. Because all preference metrics are evaluated on held-out contexts, exact-order recovery places a stronger requirement on the learned model: the recovered mechanism must preserve the full ordering generated by the ground-truth objective across unseen contexts.

The LLM-based model-discovery baselines show particularly limited recovery in the continuous setting. On discrete Clean OptFeynman, GeCCo and MDA achieve exact-order accuracies of 0.7150.715 and 0.7000.700, respectively, remaining below BL and substantially below OptScientist. On continuous Clean OptFeynman, their performance decreases sharply as the candidate set becomes denser. At K=100K=100, LLM-only, GeCCo and MDA achieve exact-order accuracies of 0.00180.0018, 0.00210.0021, and 0.00170.0017, respectively, with no perfectly recovered tasks; their pairwise accuracies remain around 0.700.70, and their dense-grid KL divergences remain around 0.640.64. A plausible interpretation is that LLM-based discovery depends strongly on the scientific and functional-form priors available in language. When such priors provide limited information about the generating mechanism, identifying a transferable law directly from observations becomes substantially more difficult. Strong textual priors may also favour familiar or plausible functional forms, creating a risk that the discovered expression reflects prior knowledge more strongly than the mechanism that generated the observations. The OptFeynman results therefore highlight the value of learning the optimization landscape from data before symbolic distillation, particularly when informative domain priors are unavailable or incomplete.

LLM baseline protocol. For the LLM-based baselines on OptFeynman, model generation, revision, and selection use only the training and validation splits. All methods use the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash model and follow their original discovery procedures with a unified budget of eight discovery rounds. To prevent semantic leakage from physics-specific notation, all OptFeynman variable names are replaced with neutral identifiers before being provided to the LLMs. The held-out test set is never exposed during model discovery or model selection. After the final model is selected, its predictive model is evaluated directly on the test set using the common OptFeynman metrics; this final evaluation is fully deterministic and involves no further LLM interaction.

Overall, the detailed statistics support the ground-truth recovery results reported in the main text. OptScientist recovers the complete preference order on most OptFeynman problems, with high pairwise agreement across the benchmark. It substantially outperforms the baseline methods in exact-order recovery, particularly in the fraction of problems for which the complete ground-truth preference order is perfectly recovered. Continuous recovery remains stable as the candidate set increases from K=10K=10 to K=100K=100, and recovery remains strong when Gaussian noise is added to the training contexts. The problem-level medians and quartiles show that these results hold across most of the benchmark optimization problems.

B.3 Human Choice under Risk and Ambiguity

B.3.1 Dataset and evaluation

The CPC18 experiment studies repeated binary choices between two monetary prospects under risk and ambiguity (Plonsky et al., 2019). We use a random split with 408,600408{,}600, 51,06051{,}060 and 51,09051{,}090 observations for training, validation and testing, respectively. For Figure 5, test metrics are first computed at the participant level and then averaged across the 686686 test participants. Error bars denote the standard error of the mean across participant-level metrics.

B.3.2 Theory Prior Agent and variable discovery

Before symbolic discovery, the Theory Prior Agent used scientific theories of decision-making under risk, ambiguity and repeated feedback to construct theoretically motivated variables beyond those directly available in the CPC18 data. These variables were specified independently of validation and test performance and were subsequently considered as candidate inputs for symbolic discovery.

Let option j∈{A,B}j\in\{A,B\} have high payoff HjH_{j}, low payoff LjL_{j}, and probability pH,jp_{H,j} of the high payoff. The agent constructed expected-value representations

EVA=pH,A​HA+(1−pH,A)​LA,EVB=pH,B​HB+(1−pH,B)​LB,\mathrm{EV}_{A}=p_{H,A}H_{A}+(1-p_{H,A})L_{A},\qquad\mathrm{EV}_{B}=p_{H,B}H_{B}+(1-p_{H,B})L_{B},

together with relative probability and payoff-dispersion measures,

Δ​pH=pH,B−pH,A,Δ​Spread=(HB−LB)−(HA−LA).\Delta p_{H}=p_{H,B}-p_{H,A},\qquad\Delta\mathrm{Spread}=(H_{B}-L_{B})-(H_{A}-L_{A}).

It also introduced an ambiguity–correlation interaction,

AmbNegCorr=Amb 1{Corr<0},\mathrm{AmbNegCorr}=\mathrm{Amb}\,\mathbbm{1}\{\mathrm{Corr}<0\},

and an indicator for the feedback framing condition,

ByFB=𝟙{Condition=ByFB}.\mathrm{ByFB}=\mathbbm{1}\{\mathrm{Condition}=\texttt{ByFB}\}.

Participant-level variables included gender,

Male=𝟙{Gender=M},\mathrm{Male}=\mathbbm{1}\{\mathrm{Gender}=\mathrm{M}\},

and an indicator for residence in wealthier regions,

WealthyRegion=𝟙{Region∈𝒲},\mathrm{WealthyRegion}=\mathbbm{1}\{\mathrm{Region}\in\mathcal{W}\},

where 𝒲\mathcal{W} denotes the corresponding region classification used in preprocessing.

Because CPC18 contains repeated choices with feedback, the Theory Prior Agent also proposed lagged obtained and forgone payoff variables. Let RtAR_{t}^{A} and RtBR_{t}^{B} denote the payoff feedback associated with options AA and BB, and let yt∈{0,1}y_{t}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether option BB was chosen. The obtained and forgone payoffs are

Rtobt=(1−yt)​RtA+yt​RtB,Rtforgone=yt​RtA+(1−yt)​RtB.R_{t}^{\mathrm{obt}}=(1-y_{t})R_{t}^{A}+y_{t}R_{t}^{B},\qquad R_{t}^{\mathrm{forgone}}=y_{t}R_{t}^{A}+(1-y_{t})R_{t}^{B}.

For prediction at round tt, only lagged quantities from preceding rounds were used. During symbolic discovery, OptScientist Model subsequently identified decision-relevant combinations of these variables, including the counterfactual payoff difference

Δ​Rtcf=Rtforgone−Rtobt.\Delta R_{t}^{\mathrm{cf}}=R_{t}^{\mathrm{forgone}}-R_{t}^{\mathrm{obt}}.

Together, the Theory Prior Agent provides candidate representations of expected reward, probability sensitivity, risk, ambiguity, framing, demographic heterogeneity and feedback, while the OptScientist Model determines how these variables enter the discovered symbolic law.

B.3.3 Direct symbolic law

For the binary-choice task presented in the CPC18 dataset, let yt=1y_{t}=1 denote choosing option B and yt=0y_{t}=0 denote choosing option A. The direct OptScientist law can be written as

U^​(xt,yt)=yt​D​(xt),y^t=arg⁡maxyt∈{0,1}​U^​(xt,yt),\widehat{U}(x_{t},y_{t})=y_{t}D(x_{t}),\qquad\widehat{y}_{t}=\arg\max_{y_{t}\in\{0,1\}}\widehat{U}(x_{t},y_{t}), (14)

where D⁡(xt)D(x_{t}) is the recovered score difference between choosing B and choosing A. The selected expression is

D⁡(xt)=\displaystyle D(x_{t})={} −0.8173​E​VA+0.5701​E​VB+0.3393​LB−0.0709​PrevForgone\displaystyle-0.8173\,EV_{A}+0.5701\,EV_{B}+0.3393\,L_{B}-0.0709\,\mathrm{PrevForgone}
−0.8173​PrevExp+1.6541​PrevChoiceB+0.0709​PrevPayoff.\displaystyle-0.8173\,\mathrm{PrevExp}+1.6541\,\mathrm{PrevChoice}_{B}+0.0709\,\mathrm{PrevPayoff}. (15)

The model predicts that people would choose option B when D⁡(xt)>0D(x_{t})>0. Continuous variables are standardized using the training split. The expression has symbolic complexity 23 and contains five distinct numerical constants.

Equation (15) supports the abstract law shown in Figure 5b. The current lottery terms form the immediate reward component V⁡(xt,yt)V(x_{t},y_{t}). The previous-choice term captures persistence in the last action, corresponding to the switching-cost component. The previous payoff and forgone-payoff terms capture sequential feedback from the previous round.

B.3.4 Automatic-feature symbolic law

AutoF OptScientist follows the automatic-feature extraction route introduced in the OptScientist Model. It first maps (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}) into an intermediate representation,

h⁡(xt,yt)=(h1,…,h8),h(x_{t},y_{t})=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{8}), (16)

taken from an OptLearner inner layer. OptDiscover then distills the final score as a symbolic function of these learned features:

s⁡(h)=\displaystyle s(h)={} 0.04345​h1+0.00976​h2+0.11970​h3+0.04345​h6+0.15760​h7\displaystyle 0.04345\,h_{1}+0.00976\,h_{2}+0.11970\,h_{3}+0.04345\,h_{6}+0.15760\,h_{7}
+0.04345​|h6|+0.11970​|0.1819​h3−0.1819​h4+0.3752​h7|−1.3408.\displaystyle+0.04345\,|h_{6}|+0.11970\,\left|0.1819\,h_{3}-0.1819\,h_{4}+0.3752\,h_{7}\right|-1.3408. (17)

The induced binary score difference is

DFM​(xt)=s⁡(h⁡(xt,1))−s⁡(h⁡(xt,0)).D_{\mathrm{FM}}(x_{t})=s\!\left(h(x_{t},1)\right)-s\!\left(h(x_{t},0)\right). (18)

The model predicts that people would choose option B when DFM​(xt)>0D_{\mathrm{FM}}(x_{t})>0. This expression has outer symbolic complexity 33 and contains seven distinct numerical constants. This automatic-feature route allows OptLearner to compress weakly structured behavioural information before symbolic extraction.

B.3.5 Predictive performance and complexity

Table 12 reports participant-level predictive performance and parameter counts for the two OptScientist variants. Direct OptScientist achieves higher choice accuracy with fewer parameters, whereas AutoF OptScientist yields slightly higher AUC and better probabilistic calibration, with lower probability MSE, NLL, KL divergence and ECE. Thus, direct symbolic discovery provides the more parsimonious decision rule, while automatic feature extraction improves the fidelity of predicted choice probabilities.

Notably, the MLP baseline achieves approximately 84% held-out accuracy. Together with the clustering of the strongest predictive models around 82–84%, this suggests that predictive performance on CPC18 is already close to saturation.

B.4 Central-Bank Monetary Policy

B.4.1 Dataset and evaluation

The central-bank experiment studies quarterly monetary-policy decisions from macro-financial conditions. The dataset contains 127127 quarterly observations. We use 9090, 2323 and 1414 observations for training, validation and out-of-time testing, respectively. The outcome is a five-class monetary policy stance yt∈{−2,−1,0,1,2}y_{t}\in\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}, ranging from large easing to large tightening.

Continuous model predictions are mapped to the observed five policy classes before computing exact policy-stance accuracy. Policy-direction accuracy compares the sign of the mapped policy class, distinguishing easing, no change and tightening. Error bars in Figure 6 are bootstrap standard errors from 10,00010{,}000 resamples of the 1414 test quarters with replacement.

B.4.5 Predictive performance and complexity

Table 13 reports held-out test performance. All uncertainty values are bootstrapped standard errors from 10,00010{,}000 quarter-level resamples with replacement. Parameter count follows the plotting convention: for neural and tree models it counts model parameters or tree capacity, whereas for symbolic models it counts distinct numerical constants in the final expression. Symbolic structural complexity is reported separately.

OptScientist shows the strongest overall out-of-time predictive performance. It attains the lowest MSE and highest R2R^{2}, exact policy-stance accuracy and direction accuracy, while symbolic regression achieves a slightly lower MAE. OptScientist-C also remains competitive, with exact and direction accuracies of 0.71430.7143 and 0.78570.7857, respectively.

Under decision-relevant structural-complexity accounting, the single-UU OptScientist law has effective complexity 131131, the constrained U/C/TU/C/T law has total effective complexity 7979, and the symbolic-regression baseline has complexity 2121. Thus, OptScientist-C yields a more compact and explicitly structured law, whereas the single-UU formulation achieves stronger out-of-time performance on most metrics. This difference may arise because the single-UU formulation retains richer state-dependent interactions and higher-order decision structure, whereas the constrained U/C/TU/C/T decomposition imposes stronger structural restrictions. These restrictions improve parsimony and interpretability, but may omit variation that remains predictive in unseen periods.

B.5 Token-Efficient Model Discovery

We provide additional details for the token-efficient model-discovery experiment in Sec. 4.4. OptScientist is compared with three LLM-based model-discovery baselines: (i) LLM-only discovery, which directly proposes and iteratively revises candidate models; (ii) GeCCo, a code-assisted LLM approach (Rmus et al., 2026); and (iii) MDA, a Bayesian experiment-design approach (Murphy, 2026). All methods use the same DeepSeek-V4-Flash (Xu et al., 2026) as the underlying language model and receive the same research description, variable information, and training data. The comparison is conducted on the CPC18 dataset and the central-bank monetary-policy dataset described in Secs. 4.2 and 4.3. For each LLM-based baseline, we evaluate maximum generation settings of 8,1928{,}192, 12,00012{,}000, 16,38416{,}384 and 24,00024{,}000 tokens per LLM call.

Evaluation protocol. Model generation, revision and selection use only the training and validation data. The held-out test set is not exposed during the discovery process and is evaluated after the final model has been selected. We record the held-out predictive accuracy of each discovered model together with cumulative LLM output-token consumption across the complete discovery run. The maximum-token setting denotes the generation limit for each individual LLM call and therefore differs from the cumulative number of generated tokens reported below.

Token accounting. We use cumulative output-token consumption as the primary measure of language-model budget. The discovery methods differ in their input representations, prompting structures and intermediate context, making input-token counts less directly comparable across approaches. Generated output tokens provide a common measure of the model-generation budget and are also the more expensive component under the API pricing used in these experiments. We additionally report held-out accuracy per output token as a descriptive summary of the accuracy–token trade-off. The analysis concerns LLM-token efficiency; training and symbolic-search computation outside the language model are not included in this measure.

Token-efficiency results. On human decisions under risk and ambiguity, the LLM-based baselines achieve closely clustered held-out accuracies while consuming between 15,77115{,}771 and 45,76145{,}761 output tokens. Notably, the strongest predictive models cluster around 82–84% held-out accuracy. Performance on the CPC18 dataset appears to saturate across all methods at approximately 83% held-out accuracy, suggesting that CPC18 poses a relatively less challenging model-discovery problem. Nevertheless, OptScientist reaches competitive held-out accuracy using 6,3966{,}396 output tokens, corresponding to 59.4%59.4\% fewer tokens than the lowest-token baseline. Its accuracy per output token is 12.961×10−512.961\times 10^{-5}, compared with a maximum of 5.260×10−55.260\times 10^{-5} among the LLM-based baselines.

On central-bank monetary-policy decisions, OptScientist achieves the highest held-out policy-stance accuracy, reaching 78.6%78.6\% with 5,9765{,}976 output tokens. The strongest LLM-based baseline reaches 70.455%70.455\% accuracy with 25,57625{,}576 output tokens, while output-token consumption across the baseline settings ranges from 16,69116{,}691 to 29,61129{,}611. Compared with the CPC18 dataset, modeling monetary-policy decisions appears more challenging for the LLM-based baselines, as the discovered models exhibit greater variability in performance. OptScientist also reaches an accuracy-per-token value of 13.153×10−513.153\times 10^{-5}, compared with a maximum of 2.962×10−52.962\times 10^{-5} among the baselines. Together, the two tasks show that OptScientist reaches competitive or stronger held-out predictive performance with substantially less LLM generation, supporting the accuracy–token-efficiency trade-off reported in Figure 7.
